The HAL archival system represents a foundational epistemic layer where scholarly documents are deposited and disseminated across institutional boundaries. This system enables GSI to construct a probabilistic model of knowledge flow, where each document's origin and credibility are weighted by institutional provenance. The mentorship influence primitive captures the personal and temporal dynamics of academic development, mapping how long-term mentorship affects thesis trajectory. In GSE, this translates into a state-transition model where academic identity evolves through mentorship arcs. The institutional credentialing primitive ensures that only documents from recognized entities contribute meaningfully to the knowledge base. These three primitives form a triadic structure: HAL provides the data layer, mentorship influences the cognitive layer, and institutional credentialing validates the epistemic layer. Failure modes include loss of institutional trust, mentorship inconsistency, and archival fragmentation. Dualities emerge in the interplay between openness (HAL) and selectivity (credentialing), and between individual agency (mentorship) and systemic structure (institutional affiliation).
